column17: The paper designs and instantiates an artefact: 'we propose a factual-driven copilot integrating LLMs with structured and semi-structured knowledge retrieval for three component types (robots, feeders and vision systems), providing a guided and traceable state-machine process for decision-making in automation equipment selection' (Abstract, p. 123). Section 2 'Copilot design' specifies the artefact; Section 3 demonstrates it in an industrial case study. No primary empirical data collection beyond the demonstration, and no purely conceptual framing.
column19: Working system exists (web application implemented in LangGraph with GPT-4o, Chroma, SQLite3, Gradio, hosted on Microsoft Azure, p. 125) and was tested by two automation engineers of an industrial partner on three ramp-up use-cases. Evaluation is limited: outcomes are a post-hoc three-band tally of 47 equipment prompts (3 / 24 / 20) against the partner's internal selections plus qualitative feedback; no defined metric, no formal protocol, no statistical treatment and no ablation or alternative-system baseline. BORDERLINE: because the tally is quantitative and compared against human selections, 'implemented-validated' is defensible; coded 'prototype' because the authors themselves describe the study as a demonstration whose 'feedback affirmed its capability' (Abstract, p. 123). R1 decision needed.
column20: Discrete manufacturing / assembly automation. Industrial partner: 'an international manufacturer of plastic products with about 850 employees, operating six factories across three continents' (Section 3, p. 125). Equipment domains covered: robotic systems, feeder technologies, machine vision systems.
column21: Automation equipment selection during production ramp-up planning. Two automation engineers tested the copilot on three ramp-up planning use-cases (two products in Europe, one in China) to derive automation components for robots, feeders and vision applications; examples in Table 1 cover pre-feeding of bushings (feeder), movement to cleaning and inspection (robot) and visual inspection (vision) (Section 3, p. 125).
column22: No numbered research questions. Stated aims: 'This research investigates whether large-language models (LLMs), combined with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), can assist in streamlining equipment selection in ramp-up planning' (Abstract, p. 123) and 'This article explores whether these recent advancements in factual-driven RAG-LLMs, combined with a state-machine architecture, can fulfill the requirements of the equipment selection process and guide automation equipment design effectively' (Section 1, p. 123).
column24: Primary mapping is 'technology-selection': the artefact selects automation technology/equipment (elementary operation -> equipment type -> specific supplier product, e.g. SCARA robot, vibratory bowl feeder, area-scan camera; Section 2 and Appendix B, Table B.1). 'factory-planning' is added as a secondary mapping because equipment/resource selection for an assembly line is a constituent task of factory planning per VDI 5200, and the paper positions the work in 'automation design, especially equipment selection' for production ramp-up (Section 1, p. 123). BOUNDARY CASE: the paper contains no investment appraisal, no site/network content, and no explicit factory-planning framework; if R1 prefers a single subdomain, 'technology-selection' alone is the safer coding. The equipment-to-attribute mapping is grounded in Boothroyd, 'Assembly Automation and Product Design' [31], a domain reference rather than a planning framework.

The core task - component-level automation equipment selection from supplier catalogs during ramp-up - is coded as 'technology-scouting' (identification of suitable technology/equipment). If R1 judges that equipment selection is not covered by any controlled term, 'other' with the specification 'automation equipment selection (component and supplier-level) for assembly ramp-up' would be the alternative.
column29: No time horizon is stated anywhere in the paper; the only temporal framing is the 'ramp-up phase when new products are integrated into production lines' (Abstract, p. 123) and 'equipment choices must be made quickly to align with market demands' (Section 1, p. 123). Strategic reading: equipment selection fixes the physical capital of the assembly system (which robot, feeder and camera are procured), i.e. a structural, investment-relevant decision. Upper-tactical reading: the decision recurs with every new product introduction into an existing line, which is the paper's explicit trigger. Coded 'ambiguous'; R1 decision needed.
column31: The decision determines which automation equipment will constitute the assembly station: the workflow maps structured requirements to an elementary operation, then to an equipment category and subtype (Robots: SCARA, articulated arm, parallel/delta, linear, cylindrical; Feeders: linear, vibratory bowl, flexible; Cameras: area scan, line scan, 3D - Table B.1), and finally to a specific supplier product (e.g. 'Epson Type: Articulated Arm Robot Model: C8-A1401 (C8XL)', Table 1, p. 125). It determines what equipment exists in the line, not how existing resources are scheduled. NOTE: the authors never use the term 'system-configuring' and do not explicitly frame the decision in those words; coded TRUE on the substance of the decision.
column34: A 'factual-driven copilot' for automation equipment selection, implemented in LangGraph as a state machine (Fig. 1) and accessible as a web application. Components: (1) a primary orchestration agent following the multi-agent design pattern of AutoGen [27]; (2) an equipment selection agent; (3) a relational (structured) knowledge system in SQLite3 mapping feeders, robots and vision systems to their attributes, linked to supplier product and equipment catalogs, with the mapping based on Boothroyd's 'Assembly Automation and Product Design' [31]; (4) a semi-structured knowledge system - a RAG component over Markdown text chunks from WZL lecture slides and dissertations on robotic systems, feeder technologies and machine vision systems, embedded with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and indexed in a Chroma vector database, chunk size 750 with overlap 150, retrieving the three most relevant chunks ranked by dot-product similarity; (5) an answer generator that synthesises the response from a defined pre-prompt. Two entry paths: general Q&A answered by the orchestration agent using both knowledge systems, or the multi-step equipment selection procedure. Selection flow: user states assembly requirements (free text or a provided template) -> requirements are analysed, structured and grouped into general assembly components via a pre-prompt -> the elementary operation (e.g. robotic handling) is determined from the structured knowledge -> a specific equipment type (e.g. Cartesian robot) is selected from structured and semi-structured knowledge -> an evaluation/selection-reflection step in which 'the LLM reflects the suitability of the decision to alleviate Hallucination' [28]; if the selection is unsuitable, additional information is requested from the user and the elementary-operation selection restarts. The orchestration agent advances to the answer generator only once all requirements are fulfilled. Infrastructure: Django REST Framework for the relational and vectorised database API, Gradio for the chat and state visualisation, Microsoft Azure hosting; the relational database is extensible via HTTP POST in a Swagger interface and the vector store via a runnable script with additional Markdown files. (Section 2, pp. 124-125.)

column36: 'OpenAI's GPT-4o model [33] is employed as the LLM model and integrated with LangGraph via its API' (Section 2, p. 125) - GPT-4o serves all LLM roles in the state machine (requirement interpretation and structuring, elementary-operation and equipment-type selection, suitability reflection, answer generation). all-MiniLM-L6-v2 is used only to generate the chunk embeddings stored in the Chroma vector database. No temperature, context length, or other decoding parameters are reported, and no model comparison is performed.

column40: The only generative model is GPT-4o, a proprietary OpenAI model accessed via API (Section 2, p. 125). AMBIGUITY: the paper explicitly describes the retrieval embedder as 'the open-source model all-MiniLM-L6-v2 by Hugging Face [36]', so under a literal reading of 'system uses both open-weight and proprietary models' the value 'mixed' could be argued. Coded 'N' because the field sits alongside model_family and the open-weight component is an embedding model, not an LLM. R1 may prefer 'mixed'.
column42: No weight updates of any kind are reported. The system relies on pre-prompts: 'The LLM interprets the term specified based on a predefined prompt (pre-prompt) but can also be reinforced through a provided template'; requirements are grouped 'based on a pre-prompt that describes them'; the answer generator 'synthesises a response with a defined pre-prompt' (Section 2, pp. 124-125). Prompt texts are not published. Fine-tuning of LLMs is only discussed as related work [23], not applied here.
column45: State-machine orchestration: the copilot 'is implemented in LangGraph [32] using a state machine model' and Fig. 1 is a 'State machine diagram of the copilot'; the authors' research question explicitly pairs 'factual-driven RAG-LLMs' with 'a state-machine architecture' (Section 1, p. 123), and the abstract calls it 'a guided and traceable state-machine process'. Recorded under 'other' because the controlled vocabulary has no state-machine/workflow-graph term.
column51: No optimisation model, objective function, decision variables, constraints or solver appear in the paper. Equipment selection is realised as rule-like retrieval and LLM reasoning over a relational attribute mapping and a RAG corpus; the only formal criterion is the dot-product relevance score used to rank retrieved chunks, which is a retrieval ranking, not an optimisation. Related work is framed against 'static rules and predefined knowledge' [9] and automated assembly process planning systems [10], not against an OR/MCDM literature. Optimisation is named only as future work: coupling equipment selection with 'the discrete-event simulation of the production systems [7]', which 'would allow for the evaluation of overall system performance across different equipment options proposed by the chatbot, with the best-performing scenario ultimately being selected' (Section 4, p. 126) - future work only, therefore not coded as present.

column53: No public dataset or benchmark. Knowledge base: Markdown text chunks from WZL lecture slides and dissertations covering robotic systems, feeder technologies and machine vision systems (chunk size 750, overlap 150, top-3 retrieval), plus a relational SQLite3 equipment-attribute mapping linked to product and equipment catalogs of the selected suppliers, with the mapping derived from Boothroyd [31]. Test material: 47 equipment prompts from three confidential internal ramp-up use-cases of the industrial partner - 'not all prompts can be shown because they involve confidential company information' (Section 3, p. 125); Table 1 shows one example prompt per component type. Neither the corpus nor the prompt set is publicly available; software available on request to the authors (Section 5 Usage Notes, p. 126).

column78: The copilot produced logical and actionable component suggestions aligned with the partner's requirements. Of 47 equipment prompts, 20 suggestions were fully suitable (all relevant requirements met), 24 were sufficient (correct subtype such as a SCARA robot plus most specific requirements such as arm length), and 3 identified only the correct equipment type but not the appropriate subtype (e.g. a feeder system but not a vibratory bowl feeder). Table 1 illustrates that copilot output can differ from the partner's choice while remaining plausible: for the robot case the partner selected Epson articulated arm robots N2-A450 whereas the copilot proposed an RNA FlexCube 380 flexible feeder, an Epson C8-A1401 (C8XL) articulated arm robot and an LMI Gocator 2150-3R-REVD laser scanner; for the vision case the partner specified area-scan cameras >5MP/30FPS and the copilot proposed an OPTRONIS CP-CYCLONE-21-230-C. Qualitative partner feedback affirmed the system's capability, and the authors emphasise traceability of recommendations derived from academic lectures, industrial literature and a supplier database. NOTE ON STUDY DESIGN: coded 'single-case' (one industrial partner, three use-cases); the results are simultaneously developer-reported, since the authors themselves classified the 47 outcomes and no independent or blinded assessment is described - R1 may prefer 'developer-reported'. No baseline system, no ablation and no statistical analysis are reported.
column81: Two coupled human-in-the-loop mechanisms. (1) Escalation on a failed self-check: after a specific equipment type is selected, 'the workflow progresses to the evaluation selection step, where the LLM reflects the suitability of the decision to alleviate Hallucination [28]. In case of an unsuitable selection, additional information about the decision is requested from the user to enhance a further iteration of the equipment selection process based on the reflection, restarting the selection of the elementary operation' (Section 2, p. 124). (2) Requirement-completeness gate: 'The primary orchestration agent advances to the answer generator only when all requirements have been fulfilled. If requirements are not yet met, it continues to obtain additional information from the relevant subcomponents as necessary' (Section 2, p. 125). The system is framed as a copilot producing 'traceable recommendations' for the automation engineer, who retains the decision, and Gradio 'visualizes the chat and the states' so the user can follow the state machine. AMBIGUITY: no explicit human approval step before an action is executed, so 'approval-gate' does not fit cleanly; the advisory copilot framing plus user-clarification loop could alternatively be coded 'other'. Coded 'escalation-protocol' because the trigger for involving the human is the system's own uncertainty/unsuitability judgement.
column85: Two complementary formalizations. (1) Structured/relational: 'The structured knowledge system maps specific equipment such as feeders, robots, and vision systems to their corresponding attributes in a relational format. It is linked to product- and equipment catalogs by the selected supplier of the respective domains. The mapping is done based on scientific books [31]' (Boothroyd, Assembly Automation and Product Design), implemented in SQLite3 and extensible via HTTP POST through a Swagger interface (Section 2, pp. 124-125). A two-level equipment taxonomy is given in Appendix B, Table B.1: Robots -> SCARA, articulated arm, parallel/delta, linear, cylindrical; Feeders -> linear, vibratory bowl, flexible; Cameras -> area scan, line scan, 3D. The selection logic also formalises intermediate 'elementary operations' (e.g. robotic handling) between requirements and equipment types. (2) Semi-structured: domain text from WZL lecture slides and dissertations normalised to Markdown, chunked (750/150) and vector-indexed in Chroma. AMBIGUITY: the authors never use the words ontology or knowledge graph, and no formal ontology language, axioms or graph structure is reported, so 'ontology' and 'knowledge-graph' would over-claim; coded 'other'. R1 may prefer 'ontology' if a typed taxonomy plus attribute schema is considered sufficient.
column86: Relational equipment-attribute schema plus a two-level equipment taxonomy (equipment category -> equipment subtype -> attributes) in SQLite3, linked to supplier product catalogs and derived from Boothroyd [31], complemented by a Markdown-normalised, vector-indexed corpus of institute lecture and dissertation material.
column89: No standardized benchmark, published rubric, or author-defined domain-specific metric is used. Outcomes are an ad-hoc, post-hoc classification of 47 prompts into three suitability bands (correct type only / correct subtype with most requirements met / fully suitable) judged informally against the industrial partner's internal selections; the bands are described in prose (Section 3, p. 125), are not named, defined, operationalised or inter-rater checked, and no accuracy or other metric is computed. AMBIGUITY: because the three bands function as an implicit ordinal scale, R1 could instead code evaluation_framework_used = TRUE with evaluation_framework_type = 'rubric'; coded FALSE here per the instruction not to infer beyond what is explicitly stated.
column92: Score 2 - key steps described but gaps remain. Reported: the state-machine workflow and its states (Fig. 1), the component decomposition, the concrete stack (LangGraph, GPT-4o via OpenAI API, Chroma, all-MiniLM-L6-v2, SQLite3, Django REST Framework, Gradio, Microsoft Azure), the RAG configuration (chunk size 750, overlap 150, top-3 chunks ranked by dot-product relevance) and the knowledge sources (WZL lecture slides and dissertations in Markdown; supplier catalogs; Boothroyd [31]). Missing for replication: all prompt and pre-prompt texts, the template offered to users, the relational schema and elementary-operation mapping, LLM decoding parameters, the 47 evaluation prompts (confidential), the procedure and criteria by which the three suitability bands were assigned and by whom, and the code (only 'available on request to the authors', Section 5, p. 126).
column94: Score 2 - prototype with limited evaluation. A working web application was deployed on Azure and used by two automation engineers of a real industrial partner on three ramp-up use-cases, and outcomes across 47 prompts were tallied against the partner's internal selections (3 / 24 / 20). However the evaluation defines no metric, uses no baseline system, ablation or statistical test, rests on a single partner and on author-performed outcome classification, and is summarised by the authors themselves as 'promising feedback' (Section 4, p. 126). This is more than a framework-only paper but short of 'implemented + quantitative evaluation' in the strict sense; consistent with validation_status = 'prototype'. If R1 codes validation_status as 'implemented-validated', this dimension should be raised to 3.
